Session 3 new: jit_gate_pass on auto gates returns 'Passed' even when the underlying run fails — always inspect jit gate check-all after jit_gate_pass to see the real outcome. Example: I called jit_gate_pass code-review on 91c06222 commit 17b6fa4 and got 'Passed gate code-review' back, but jit_gate_check-all showed the gate actually FAILED with the docs finding. The tool return is misleading; the gate-runs are the ground truth.

Session 4 new: jit_gate_pass MCP call has a 10-minute tool-level timeout; ai-review.sh for a 2260-line module takes 7-10+ min and may exceed it. The MCP timeout kills the subprocess AND records no gate run (no result.json folder). Workaround: invoke `jit gate pass <issue> code-review` via Bash with `run_in_background=true` and a 15-minute timeout, then poll `.jit/gate-runs/` directory listings for the new run folder. Never assume MCP success === gate run completed.

Session 4 new: For expression-template / delayed-reduction fused-vs-eager performance, the speedup ceiling at n=1024 over Mersenne-31 is extremely thin. Allocation cost is amortised over 3 seconds of compute (ratio ~10⁻³). A 'measurably faster at n=1024' criterion cannot be met by blocking alone; it requires either SIMD vectorisation inside the inner loop, Strassen recursion, or a structurally different memory layout. Lesson for future criterion-writing: if the criterion is about runtime wins at a specific size, require an order-of-magnitude justification before signing it [hard].

Session 4 new: When prescribing a rework, do NOT offer 'either write a proper blocked kernel OR amend the criterion' as worker-visible options. That leaks the scope decision to the worker, who will sometimes pick the cheapest option (amend the doc). Keep worker prompts strictly about code changes; keep scope decisions in lead ↔ user escalation. Session 4 ultimately did this correctly by using AskUserQuestion before dispatching R3 rework, but the R2 prompt's option-list style (per Fix A's 'either A/B/C') is a footgun for future rounds.

Session 4 new: Commit `e94eb23` preserves the blocked kernel rewrite even though the gate isn't closed. This is intentional: the rewrite is a strict performance improvement (4.4% faster fused path) that should NOT be reverted when the user finalises the scope decision. If the user picks 'aspirational', commit e94eb23 stays and the bench md gets updated with honest numbers. If the user picks 'kernel-rewrite again', we already have T1's blocking exhausted — the next lever is SIMD or a different approach, neither of which fits T2's scope.
